about.title: Santa Barbara Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Santa Barbara is a city of roughly 91,842 people, and most residents will trust a doctor, nurse, or surgeon here at some point in their lives. That trust is usually rewarded. Occasionally it is not, and the person left living with the consequences has to figure out what happened and what to do next. That is where a malpractice claim begins, and it is rarely simple. California's MICRA law shapes every step: a claim generally must be filed within one year of discovering the harm and never more than three years after the injury, a 90-day notice must go to the provider before suit, and a qualified medical expert is almost always needed to explain how the care fell below the standard. The law also caps non-economic damages, though that cap rises each year. LawProactive is not a law firm. We are a free service that connects Santa Barbara County residents with an independent attorney who handles these cases on contingency, so you owe nothing unless there is a recovery.

items.question: My surgery in Santa Barbara did not go the way I hoped. Is that malpractice?
items.answer: Not by itself. Medicine carries real risks, and California law is clear that a disappointing outcome alone does not make a provider liable. A claim depends on showing the care fell below what a reasonably careful provider would have done, which is why a qualified medical expert almost always has to weigh in. An independent attorney can review your records and tell you whether that standard appears to have been met.

items.question: How long do I have to file a medical malpractice claim in California?
items.answer: Under MICRA, you generally have one year from the date you discovered, or reasonably should have discovered, the injury, and in most situations no more than three years from the date the injury happened. You also have to give the provider written notice at least 90 days before filing suit. Because those periods overlap, it helps to talk with an attorney well before either one runs out.

items.question: Is there a limit on what I can recover in a Santa Barbara malpractice case?
items.answer: California caps non-economic damages, meaning things like pain, suffering, and loss of enjoyment of life, in medical malpractice cases. That cap is not fixed; it rises each year under the current law. Economic losses such as medical bills and lost wages are handled separately. The attorney you connect with can explain how these rules apply to your specific situation without promising any particular result.
